articles.headline: Gemini for Mac can now operate your apps and files, with a live preview you can pause, stop or approve
articles.excerpt: Google added computer use to the Gemini desktop app, letting the agent work across native Mac apps, local files and the web in the background.
summary: Google announced on Thursday that the Gemini app for macOS can now take over multistep work on a user's computer. Given an instruction, the agent can move between native Mac apps, local files and websites to do things like fill out forms, repeat an operation across a batch of files, sort documents into folders by rules the user sets, or assemble a slideshow from files and online dashboards. It launches in English, in the US only, for Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers.

The interaction model is the interesting part: the agent works inside a live preview embedded in the chat, so the user's own screen and cursor stay free for other work while it runs, and the person can pause it, stop it or approve actions before they happen. Google is arriving after OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, which already ship desktop agents, and the launch follows last week's expansion of Gemini's Tasks feature. Google has not said when other markets or platforms will get it.
articles.whyItMatters: A contained live preview with pause, stop and pre-approval controls is becoming the default way to show an agent working on someone's behalf, so expect users to look for the same pattern in any product where agents act.
articles.author: Sarah Perez
articles.imageAlt: Gemini chat asking to model a butterfly sketch in Blender with computer use, showing its step list and a live Mac preview

articles.headline: OpenAI starts testing its always-on Dots agents with some $20 ChatGPT Plus users
articles.excerpt: Dots, previously limited to Pro and higher tiers, are reaching a small group of Plus users and all Business Standard accounts.
summary: OpenAI has begun offering Dots, its proactive agents that keep working on tasks when the user is away, to a small number of ChatGPT Plus subscribers, ChatGPT engineering lead Thibault Sottiaux said on X. All ChatGPT Business Standard users are getting access as well. Until now Dots were reserved for Pro and higher plans. They can use more than 4,000 apps through OpenAI's plugin ecosystem and can connect to a user's PC to operate it, with progress visible by opening the Dot's own computer view.

Dots originally ran on GPT-6 Astra and can now also use GPT-6.1 Terra. Recent additions include iOS widgets, Shortcuts support, iMessage and RCS messaging, and replying to a Dot straight from an iOS notification. On Pro and Business Premium, simple Dot conversations don't count toward usage limits; OpenAI hasn't said whether that applies to the new tiers, or whether Plus access is permanent.
articles.whyItMatters: Background agents that report through widgets, notifications and messaging threads move the agent experience out of the chat window, so status and reply surfaces need as much design attention as the main app.
articles.author: Steve Dent
articles.imageAlt: Phone showing the OpenAI Dots logo in front of a colorful Dots wordmark

articles.headline: The Black Box in Your Pocket: show a checkable reason with every consequential AI decision
articles.excerpt: Tushar Deshmukh argues opacity is a design choice, and that users who feel they understand an AI verdict usually don't.
summary: In part seven of his Designing the Machine series for UX Magazine, Tushar Deshmukh argues that people don't need to know how a model works internally; they need a reason they can verify before a decision hurts them. Every model encodes choices about what to optimize and which data to trust, he writes, and whether a product exposes those choices is a design decision rather than an unavoidable cost of complexity. He leans on the illusion of explanatory depth, the bias that makes people feel they understand something they can't actually explain, to argue that users won't ask for transparency on their own.

His recommendations: attach a clear reason code to every consequential output, as credit bureaus have long done with scores; make the explanation part of the main interface rather than a settings page written for auditors; treat regulatory disclosures such as India's algo-trading rules or the EU AI Act as a minimum; and listen for users who accept a decision while saying they don't know why it happened. His test for a good explanation is whether the user can correctly predict what the system would do if the inputs changed slightly.
articles.whyItMatters: Pair every consequential agent action with a short, checkable reason in the main UI, and test it by asking users to predict what the agent would do if one input changed.
articles.author: Tushar Deshmukh
articles.imageAlt: UX Magazine title card for Designing the Machine part 7 with the line Show the reason behind the decision

articles.headline: Canva adds a switch to turn off its generative AI tools and see less AI content
articles.excerpt: Free and paid users can now disable Magic Write, Magic Design, Dream Lab and other generative features from settings.
summary: Canva now lets users switch off its generative AI features with a single setting under Profile, Settings, Permission. The toggle disables tools such as Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code and AI Shapes, plus image generation in Canva's chatbot. A second option under AI personalization pushes human-made templates and graphics to the top of library searches. Both settings are available on free and paid plans.

Not everything goes away: the background remover and Magic Grab stay on because, in Canva's words, they speed up everyday work without generating anything new. Canva says only a small part of its library is AI-generated and that designs using those elements carry an AI label in their metadata. The change follows years of requests from users frustrated by the flood of AI features since 2023, and comes a month after Canva launched its in-house image model, Craft.
articles.whyItMatters: Canva separates assistive AI from generative AI and lets users opt out of the second, a useful model for products where some users want AI help and others want none.
articles.author: Emma Roth

articles.headline: Figma's image tools now generate up to six drafts or compare three models side by side
articles.excerpt: Make image and Edit image can return two, four or six results from one prompt, or one result each from up to three models.
summary: Figma's November 18 update lets its AI image tools produce several candidates at once. In Make image and Edit image, designers can ask for two, four or six images from a single prompt, or pick up to three models, each of which returns one image from the same prompt. Figma's credit guide lists GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, NanoBanana 2 Lite and NanoBanana 2 among the models. Reference images can steer the direction, hovering over a candidate previews it on the selected layer, and Place all on canvas drops every result onto the canvas for comparison.

The feature works on all plans for people with edit access, though on the Starter plan it is limited to Figma Design. Every generation draws on the AI credits shared with Figma's other AI features, and the cost depends on which models are chosen and how many images are requested, so comparing models side by side spends credits faster than a single prompt.
articles.whyItMatters: Side-by-side multi-model output on the canvas turns model choice into a visual comparison, a pattern worth borrowing wherever users must pick between AI results.
articles.author: Jongmin Park
articles.imageAlt: A real design canvas comparing the results generated by the Figma AI image model. © Figma

articles.headline: Luke Wroblewski on design by playground: disposable tools built with coding agents
articles.excerpt: Instead of static mockups, designers can have an agent build a one-off tool with live controls for a single design question.
summary: Luke Wroblewski argues that designers are starting to build their own narrow, throwaway design tools with AI coding agents, an approach he calls design by playground. A playground is a small live interface with adjustable variables, where a designer can compare variants such as short, long or missing text, tweak size, weight and color, and interact with the result directly. His post shows playgrounds for background animations, email notifications, brand assets and exporting PDFs from Figma files, including one he built to decide how much of an agent's reasoning, tool use, delegation and monitoring to show in an app.

The advantages over mockups, he writes, are real content and data that expose edge cases early, timing and loading, empty and error states turned into controls, and running in the product's actual environment with real fonts, scrolling, touch and performance. Chosen values can be exported as code or tokens for engineers or coding agents. Playgrounds used to cost more than they were worth; coding agents now build one in minutes, so it can be used for an afternoon and thrown away.
articles.whyItMatters: A quick playground with sliders for how much agent reasoning and activity to show is a cheap way to settle transparency debates with real states instead of static frames.
articles.author: Luke Wroblewski
articles.imageAlt: Playground app with a particle simulation canvas and a side panel of behavior sliders and dropdowns

articles.headline: From prototype to pull request: what it takes for designers' AI-built work to ship
articles.excerpt: Jacquelyn Halpern lays out the workflow, guardrails and team setup that let design prototypes become reviewed code.
summary: Jacquelyn Halpern, who leads product design and AI at Salesforce Trailhead, writes that the conversation about AI prototyping has moved from how fast designers can build something to whether that work can become part of the product. Her workflow: explore in code with tools like Cursor, Claude Code, Figma Make or Codex; give the agent the real components, tokens, docs and repository conventions; design for missing data, permission limits, failed requests and keyboard use; preview in staging with test accounts; and open a draft pull request for engineers to review and merge.

She cites Stripe's internal Protodash system, Atlassian's CLI, MCP server and skills for its design system, Salesforce's SLDS 2, a Doctolib fix that shipped from a designer's draft PR, and Big Medium's shared repository. Her advice to teams: make design systems readable by agents, set up repository and staging access, define what a good contribution includes and who owns it after release, build designers' code literacy, keep room for throwaway exploration, and measure outcomes rather than lines of generated code.
articles.whyItMatters: Teams letting designers ship through pull requests need agreed rules on states, review and ownership, or AI-built prototypes stay demos.
articles.author: Jacquelyn Halpern
articles.imageAlt: UX Magazine interaction design title card reading A prototype can continue into the product

articles.headline: LATO raises $4.7M for AI agents that recruit and interview customers and experts
articles.excerpt: The startup's agents run interviews in participants' own languages and blend the findings with desk research and client data.
summary: LATO, founded by Tymek Staniszewski and Tien Chu, has raised a $4.7 million seed round co-led by Air Street Capital and Axiom Partners, with Y Combinator, Montis VC, Inception Fund and angels including Paul Graham. Its AI agents find and interview customers and industry experts in their own languages, then combine what they hear with published research and a client's internal data. Recordings and transcripts stay available for review, and investment firms such as Verdane, Blume Equity and North Island have used it for commercial due diligence.

Investors use the output to size markets, analyze competitors and test pricing, including how customers might react to a price rise. LATO plans to spend the money on engineering, research and sales, to let its agents run a wider range of studies on their own, and to look beyond investors at consultancies and companies testing demand before entering a market. The pitch is speed: deal timelines decide how much time there is to understand a market.
articles.whyItMatters: AI-moderated interviews are moving from UX tools into adjacent research markets, which raises the bar for how researchers vet recruiting, consent and transcript quality when an agent runs the session.
articles.author: Tamara Djurickovic
articles.imageAlt: LATO co-founders seated at a table in an office, talking

articles.headline: Stop renting your own memory: treat design decisions as owned, expiring, verifiable knowledge
articles.excerpt: Pavel Bukengolts proposes an operating model and a 30-day context-tax audit so teams own their institutional knowledge.
summary: In a long UX Magazine essay, Pavel Bukengolts of UX Design Lab argues that AI search shrinks the advantage of long-tenured staff and big agencies, but only helps if a team's knowledge is liquid, meaning it reaches the people who need it, and trusted, meaning it is current, owned and verified. Otherwise retrieval just surfaces stale or contradictory answers faster. He calls the cost of scattered, undocumented context a context tax and warns that vendors can create lock-in by owning the indexes, embeddings and taxonomies even when the documents belong to the client.

His operating model has a small internal core that owns decisions, a systems enablement squad that maintains the source-of-truth map and decision logs, and an elastic edge of freelancers and partners. Practices include capturing decisions as a by-product of work, giving each one a rationale, owner, risk and expiry date, letting accessibility exceptions lapse unless renewed, verifying high-risk items by hand, and resolving conflicts with the rule that evidence wins and owners decide. He suggests starting with a 30-day audit of time-to-context and reuse.
articles.whyItMatters: Decision logs with owners and expiry dates are as useful to AI assistants as to people, since stale design rationale is exactly what retrieval will surface confidently.
articles.author: Pavel Bukengolts
articles.imageAlt: UX Magazine title card for the essay Stop Renting Your Own Memory

articles.headline: Microsoft merges To Do and Planner into unified plans that work inside Copilot and Cowork
articles.excerpt: One task system now spans Outlook, Teams, Planner and Loop, with Planner Agent and an MCP server built on top.
summary: Microsoft's Planner team announced unified tasks and plans, a single system for personal, team and organization-wide work across Outlook, Teams, Planner and Loop. The plans also show up in Microsoft Copilot and Cowork, with Autopilot support planned. Goals view, Timeline view and custom fields have already shipped as premium features, which need a Copilot, Planner Plan 1 or Planner and Project Plan 3 license; sprints, backlogs, task hierarchy and dependencies are on the roadmap. Recent additions include task chat, Capacity view, custom templates and views, and task history.

With a Copilot add-on, Planner Agent can carry out tasks in a plan and write status reports, Copilot users can manage tasks from chat, and the Planner plugin lets Cowork act across plans. A Planner MCP server, part of Work IQ, connects unified plans to custom agent workflows, and Graph APIs for unified tasks are in beta. The To Do apps retire on June 30, 2027, with new personal tasks stored in a private Planner plan; premium plans stay supported during the transition.
articles.whyItMatters: Microsoft is collapsing personal to-dos, team plans and goals into one task model that agents can read and write, raising expectations for how unified and agent-ready a work-management data model must be.
articles.author: Ashna Patel
articles.imageAlt: Four colleagues talking around a laptop in an office

articles.headline: Meta employees say its Muse agent mixed up conversations and surfaced others' private data
articles.excerpt: Internal posts describe Muse showing strangers' bank balances, childcare requests and orders, according to a Reuters investigation.
summary: Reuters reported that Meta employees testing Muse, the company's personal AI agent, raised internal alarms that it was mixing up conversations between accounts. Staff described seeing childcare requests, career advice and product orders they never made, plus bank balances that weren't theirs; in one case Muse volunteered two account balances in the middle of a chat about weather and tides. Another employee said Muse reminded her to answer her sister's Signal message even though she had never connected other apps, calling it an extreme privacy violation.

Meta said employee testing is central to development and that staff run different versions of Muse with features the public doesn't have. It's not clear how widespread the mix-ups are. Muse launched in September and has passed 10 million downloads, making it one of the fastest-growing apps on record; the report adds to earlier privacy complaints about the agent.
articles.whyItMatters: Agents with long memory and cross-app access need visible boundaries around whose data they're using, because one leaked detail can break trust in the whole product.
articles.author: Aisha Malik
articles.imageAlt: Fuzzy Muse mascot character wearing headphones at a desk with a laptop and phone

articles.headline: Google built a mirror-world internet to train Chrome's browsing agents safely
articles.excerpt: The Mirror Dimension is a closed web of fake shops, social sites and bank dashboards where agents face hidden prompt injections.
summary: Google's Chrome team has detailed the Mirror Dimension, an isolated web environment it fully controls for training and testing Gemini-powered browsing agents. It contains a wide range of realistic sites, including social networks, shops and bank dashboards, which agents must use through real Chrome the way they would on the open web, while facing resilience tests such as hidden prompt-injection attacks. The team built the sites with fleets of web-development agents guided by a custom harness, down to details like promo codes and populated social feeds.

Engineers say the approach addresses eval awareness, where models behave differently when they detect a test, and the risk of letting unrefined agents loose online. Chrome AI security engineer Charles Qian said agents have started showing better judgment about what information a task needs and when to hand back to the user for confirmation. Google plans to open the environment to other internal teams and is sharing the method in the hope other companies adopt it.
articles.whyItMatters: Knowing when an agent should stop and ask the user is being trained, not just designed, so confirmation points in the UI should match how the agent is evaluated.
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman
articles.imageAlt: Illustration of mirrored walking figures with cursors on their heads against bold blue, yellow and red bands

articles.headline: Microsoft AI ships seven MAI models at Ignite, pitching near-frontier quality at a fraction of the price
articles.excerpt: The lineup spans coding, cyber defense, image generation, real-time speech, medical transcription and model routing.
summary: Microsoft AI announced seven models at Ignite. MAI Code 2, now in GitHub Copilot, is said to reach 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's average benchmark score at about 40% of the price, and MAI Code 2 Flash targets routine coding. MAI Image 2.7 ranks first for image editing on Artificial Analysis, with a Flash version priced around $10 per 1,000 images in Foundry. MAI Realtime 1 is a speech-to-speech model from $0.01 per audio minute, and MAI Cyber 2 Flash targets security work.

The list also includes Dragon Copilot Transcribe for clinical conversations and Decision 1.1, a router that sends requests to larger models only when needed. Microsoft also unveiled its Maia 200 accelerator and MAI Licensed Weights, which let customers customize a frontier MAI model and run it in their own Azure tenant. All performance and price comparisons come from Microsoft's own evaluations.
articles.whyItMatters: Cheap, fast in-house models and routers make it realistic to run AI on routine work-management tasks at scale, which changes which agent features are affordable to ship broadly.
articles.imageAlt: Ignite '26 wordmark on a soft blue and gold gradient
